conversation.content: Let's design a video streaming platform like YouTube or Netflix. Users can upload videos and other users can watch them. What questions do you have?
Sure. How many users are we expecting? And do we need to support live streaming or just pre-recorded videos?
100 million monthly active users. Pre-recorded videos only. 500,000 new video uploads per day. 1 million concurrent viewers at peak. What else do you want to know?

Okay, that's a lot of users. I think we'd need a pretty big system. Let me start with the upload flow. A user uploads a video through our app, it goes to our server, and we store it. Then when someone wants to watch it, we serve the video file to them.
That's a high-level sketch. Let's dig in. When a user uploads a 4K video, how does it become available in different quality levels — 1080p, 720p, 480p?

Well... the video just... plays in different qualities? I mean, the player probably adjusts the quality based on the user's internet speed. Maybe we store the video and the player handles downscaling it on the fly?

Not quite. The player can't downscale a 4K video in real-time on a mobile phone — that would be extremely CPU-intensive. We need to pre-process the video on the server side. This process is called transcoding. Have you heard of it?
Oh, transcoding. Right, I've heard the term. So we convert the original video into multiple resolutions? Like creating separate files for 1080p, 720p, 480p?

Exactly. Each resolution is a separate encoded file. And it's not just resolution — we also create different bitrates and sometimes different codecs. For a single uploaded video, we might generate 15-20 different versions. How would you architect the transcoding pipeline?

I guess we'd have a server that takes the uploaded video and runs FFmpeg on it to create all those versions. We'd store the results in S3 or something. Maybe we'd need a few servers since 500,000 uploads a day is a lot of videos to process.

You're on the right track with FFmpeg and S3, but 'a few servers' is underselling it. If each video takes 10 minutes to transcode and we have 500K uploads per day, how many transcoding workers do we need?

Let me think... 500,000 videos at 10 minutes each is 5 million minutes of transcoding per day. A day has 1,440 minutes. So one server can do 144 videos per day. We'd need... 500,000 divided by 144... about 3,500 servers? That seems like a lot.

The math is directionally right, though in practice you'd split a video into chunks and transcode in parallel to reduce wall-clock time. But yes, transcoding is compute-intensive. Now let's talk about playback. How does a user's video player get the video data?
The player would make a request to our server and we'd stream the video file back. We could use a CDN to cache popular videos closer to users so they load faster.
CDN is right. But how does the player know which quality to request? And what happens when the user's bandwidth changes mid-video?
The player could check the internet speed at the start and pick the best quality? And if bandwidth drops... maybe it buffers until the connection improves?

There's a standard protocol for this called adaptive bitrate streaming — HLS or DASH. The video is split into small segments, usually 2-10 seconds each. The player downloads a manifest file that lists all available quality levels and their segment URLs. It starts with a quality level based on estimated bandwidth, then continuously monitors download speed. If bandwidth drops, the next segment is fetched at a lower quality — seamlessly, without buffering. Does that make sense?

Oh, that's clever. So the video is actually broken into small chunks, and each chunk exists in multiple qualities. The player dynamically switches between them. That explains why on YouTube sometimes the quality drops and then comes back. So we'd need our transcoding pipeline to also segment the video?
Exactly. Now let's talk about storage. With 500K uploads per day and 15-20 transcoded versions each, how much storage do you need?

Hmm. If an average original video is... maybe 1GB? And we create 15 versions at different qualities, the total might be 3-4x the original size because lower quality versions are smaller. So about 4GB per video? Times 500K uploads... that's 2 petabytes per day? That can't be right.

Your per-video estimate isn't unreasonable for longer videos, but the average upload is shorter — think 5-10 minutes, not feature films. Still, storage is massive. This is why platforms like YouTube use tiered storage — hot videos on fast storage or CDN, warm on standard S3, cold on Glacier. How would you decide what's hot versus cold?

Makes sense. I'd look at view count and recency. Videos uploaded in the last week or with high view counts stay on the CDN and fast storage. Older videos with low views get moved to cheaper storage. We could have a background job that checks view counts and migrates videos between tiers.
Good intuition. What about the metadata side — video titles, descriptions, user info, comments? How do you store and serve that?

I'd use a regular database for that. Probably MySQL or Postgres. A videos table with title, description, upload_date, user_id, view_count. A users table. A comments table. Standard relational stuff. For the video feed or search, maybe we'd add Elasticsearch on top.
We're running low on time. What do you think are the biggest challenges in building this system?

I think the scale of storage is the biggest challenge — petabytes of video data. And making sure videos load fast for users around the world, so the CDN strategy is important. Also handling the upload and processing pipeline reliably so no videos get lost.
Thank you. There's more we could have explored — content delivery optimization, DRM, video recommendations — but we covered the core flow. Thanks for your time.

strengths: Receptive to interviewer guidance — incorporated new concepts when taught
Attempted capacity estimation math even when unsure of numbers
weaknesses: No understanding of transcoding — fundamental to video streaming architecture
Did not know adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH) which is core to the domain
Never discussed failure handling, content protection, or API design
Shallow answers throughout — rarely went beyond surface-level descriptions
